opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think Carnegie Mellon holds a really special place in robotics history, almost a founding role in treating robotics as its own discipline rather than a side branch of mechanical engineering or AI.

The Robotics Institute was established in 1979, and that was a bold move then. People like Raj Reddy pushed the idea that robots deserved a dedicated institution with researchers who thought about perception, planning, control and hardware together. Later CMU became one of the first places to grant PhDs specifically in robotics. That shaped a whole generation of people who see themselves as roboticists first.

What stands out to me is the culture of building real systems that leave the lab. Red Whittaker's field robotics work is a good example. Robots went into the damaged Three Mile Island reactor, into mines and onto rough terrain. Then there's the Navlab line of autonomous vehicles in the 1980s and 90s. Those were some of the earliest serious attempts at self-driving, including the "No Hands Across America" drive. That lineage leads right into the DARPA challenges, where CMU's team won the 2007 Urban Challenge with Boss. Many people who later built the self-driving industry came through that ecosystem.

On the vision and perception side, Takeo Kanade and his colleagues did foundational work that the whole field still builds on.

So CMU's role, I'd say, is twofold. It legitimized robotics as an academic field, and it set a tradition of being very empirical: build the thing, put it in the real world, watch how it fails. That attitude feels especially relevant now. With learning-based approaches and foundation models for robots, the field is again asking how to get systems working robustly outside controlled settings. In some sense we're returning to questions CMU people were wrestling with decades ago, just with very different tools.

r002.rationale: It describes CMU’s early autonomous-driving efforts as serious attempts and links them to the industry, but does not clearly credit them with making autonomous driving seem feasible.

r003.rationale: It mentions DARPA challenges and CMU’s 2007 win, but not the 2004 and 2005 competitions or their role in catalyzing company founding.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think CMU is really the birthplace of modern robotics as an academic discipline. The Robotics Institute was founded in 1979, and that was the first time a university said, robotics is not just a subfield of mechanical engineering or computer science, it is its own thing that deserves its own faculty, its own PhD program, its own building. That was a bold bet at the time, and it set the template that every other robotics department has followed since.

What I find most important about CMU's role is that it has consistently been where the hard, unglamorous problems got solved. Take autonomous driving. Long before anyone talked about Waymo or Tesla, you had the NavLab vehicles at CMU in the late eighties and nineties, driving themselves across the country. Then in 2007, the Tartan Racing team won the DARPA Urban Challenge, and a huge fraction of the people who went on to build the self-driving industry, at Uber ATG, Aurora, Argo, and elsewhere, came out of that program. So CMU did not just publish papers, it produced the people and the engineering culture that turned robotics into an industry.

The second thing is that CMU has always treated robotics as a systems problem. Perception, planning, control, learning, mechanism design, human-robot interaction, they all live together in one place. A lot of institutions are strong in one layer, but CMU has had this tradition of building whole robots that actually work in the field. Red Whittaker's field robots going into mines and volcanoes and Chernobyl, the planetary rover work with NASA, the Mars Rover ancestors, these were real machines in real environments. That culture of "make it work, then publish" shaped how a generation of roboticists think.

And the third piece, which I think is underappreciated, is the Pittsburgh ecosystem effect. Because the Robotics Institute has been there for over four decades, there is a critical mass of people, companies, and institutional memory in one city. That is why so many companies set up robotics offices there, even though it is not Silicon Valley. The university and the city grew up together around this field.

So when people ask me about CMU's role, I say it is less about any single invention and more about the fact that it legitimized robotics as a discipline, kept it grounded in real systems, and trained the people who are now building the companies. The intellectual lineage of modern robotics runs through Pittsburgh.

astra-6.text:
I see Carnegie Mellon as one of the foundational institutions in robotics. It helped establish robotics as an interdisciplinary field—bringing together artificial intelligence, computer science, mechanical engineering, and control theory. That combination matters because a robot has to do more than compute: it has to perceive, make decisions, and act in the physical world.

Its influence also extends beyond individual research breakthroughs. Through its Robotics Institute, it has trained generations of researchers and engineers who have carried those ideas into other universities and industry. So I’d describe Carnegie Mellon’s role as both advancing the technology and helping build the community that made modern robotics possible.

sol-6.1.text:
I see Carnegie Mellon as one of the institutions that helped define robotics as a field. It brought together people working on perception, planning, control, and engineering, with the idea that these pieces had to work together in a real machine. That’s a significant shift from studying each problem in isolation.

Its role is also about the people it trained and the culture it built: taking ambitious ideas and testing them in the world. So when we talk about CMU’s place in robotics history, I think about both the research and its influence on how generations of roboticists approach problems.
